Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:78: The pious Rabbi Lefidot, peace be upon him, testified to my master, may his rest be in Eden, that he saw in a dream the pious sage Rabbi Yehudah bar Shushan, peace be upon him, after his passing, here in the Upper Galilee, and saw that his face shone like the light of the sun, and every single hair of his beard shone as if it were a torch. He asked him by what merit he attained this, and he said to him: through the virtue of silence that he possessed, for in all his days he never spoke idle speech. This shows that study is not the essential thing but rather action.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:79: Regarding the death of infants, they elaborated at length in the Zohar, parashat Mishpatim, and the exposition is lengthy; see there. This aspect belongs to the matter of judgment and fear, and we chose to include it in this Gate in order to incorporate fear within love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:80: Another of the things that induce and arouse a person to love his Creator is when he contemplates what the Holy One, blessed be He, promised through the prophets and the words of the holy spirit concerning the goodness of the World to Come that He is destined to grant the righteous as an inheritance. The prophet Isaiah said (Isaiah 4:5): "And the Lord will create over every dwelling of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day and smoke, and the brightness of a flaming fire by night, for over all the glory there shall be a canopy." And in the Zohar (parashat Vayakhel, from p. 209 to p. 213) they elaborated at length on the matters of Gan Eden, and explained this verse there; and our sages, of blessed memory (Bava Batra ch. 5, 75a), explained this verse, in these words: "'And the Lord will create over every dwelling of Mount Zion and over her assemblies' — Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to make seven canopies for every single righteous person in Gan Eden, as it is said, 'And the Lord will create over every dwelling of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day,' etc., 'for over all the glory there shall be a canopy.' Rabbi Yochanan said: this teaches that for every single righteous person the Holy One, blessed be He, makes a canopy according to his honor. And why do I need 'smoke' at the canopy? Rabbi Chanina the Great said: because each one's canopy is scorched by his fellow's canopy — woe for that shame, woe for that disgrace!" — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:81: Further, on the secret of this verse, the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, parashat Vayechi, beginning of p. 219) — this being the end of the passage we quoted in the Gate of Fear, chapter 2 — in these words: "We have learned: after seven days, the body is as it was, and its soul enters its place, entering the Cave of Machpelah; it sees what it sees, and enters the place it enters, until it reaches Gan Eden, and it encounters the Cherubim and the blade of the sword that is in the lower Gan Eden. If it is meritorious to enter, it enters. We have learned: four supports stand ready, one image of the body in their hands, and it is clothed in it with joy, and sits in that dwelling until the appointed time. Afterward a herald calls, and the pillar of three colors is made ready, and that pillar is called 'the dwelling of Mount Zion,' as it is written (Isaiah 4:5), 'And the Lord will create over every dwelling of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day and smoke, and the brightness of a flaming fire' — it ascends by that pillar to the Gate of Righteousness of Zion, and Jerusalem is in it. If it merits to ascend further, better is its portion and lot, to cling within the King's own body; and if it does not merit to ascend further, it is written (ibid. 4:3), 'And it shall be, whoever remains in Zion and is left in Jerusalem shall be called holy.' And if it merits to ascend still further, happy is he who merits the honor of the King and to delight in the supernal delight above, in the place called 'heaven,' as it is written (Isaiah 58:14), 'Then you shall delight in the Lord' — precisely 'in the Lord.' Happy is the portion of one who merits to Chesed, as it is written (Psalms 57:11), 'For Your kindness is great unto the heavens' — is it only unto the heavens? But it is written (Psalms 108:5), 'For Your kindness is great above the heavens'! Rabbi Yosi said: there is Chesed and there is Chesed — supernal Chesed and lower Chesed. Supernal Chesed is above the heavens; lower Chesed is that of which it is written (Isaiah 55:3), 'the sure mercies of David,' and of these it is written 'unto the heavens.'" — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:82: Further, regarding the greatness of Gan Eden, the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, parashat Chayei Sarah, pp. 129-130), in these words: "Come and see: one who sanctifies and guards himself in this world so that he is not defiled — his dwelling in that world is among those holy supernal ones who perform service constantly, and these stand in the 'courtyard,' as in the phrase, 'the courtyard of the Tabernacle.' And there are others who are more inward, who are not in the courtyard but in the house itself, as in the phrase (Psalms 65:5), 'we shall be satisfied with the goodness of Your house' — David said 'we shall be satisfied with the goodness of Your house'; but since he said 'may he dwell in Your courts,' why does it then say 'we shall be satisfied with the goodness of Your house'? It should have said 'satisfied with goodness,' corresponding to 'may he dwell'! Rather, we have learned: there is no sitting in the Temple courtyard except for the kings of the House of David alone, and there is a place for the supernal pious ones who enter within — and who are they? As it is written, 'and those who camp before the Tabernacle, to the east, before the Tent of Meeting, eastward, Moses and Aaron and his sons.' And there are many dwellings upon dwellings, and lights upon lights, distinguished in that world, and each one is abashed by the light of his fellow — just as deeds are distinguished in this world, so places and lights are distinguished in that world." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:83: Regarding the ranks of the righteous in Gan Eden, they elaborated at length in the Yalkut, part 1 (parashat Bereishit, siman 20, p. 6c), on the verse (Genesis 2:8), "And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, to the east"; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:84: They further said, of blessed memory, in the Sifrei (on Devarim, siman 10) on the verse (Psalms 16:11), "fullness of joys [sova semachot] is Your presence" — do not read "sova semachot" [fullness of joys] but "sheva semachot" [seven joys]. The faces of the righteous are destined in the future to resemble the sun, the moon, the firmament, the stars, lightning, roses, and the menorah of the Temple, etc. — and they brought a verse for each and every one there; and likewise in the Midrash Vayikra Rabbah this passage is brought on the verse "and you shall take for yourselves"; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:85: When a person contemplates the goodness of the World to Come — how wondrous and hidden a matter it is, of which it is said (Isaiah 64:3), "No eye has seen, O God, besides You, what He will do for one who waits for Him" — it is fitting that he improve his deeds and love his Maker, since out of His great kindness He will grant him a portion of that supernal pleasantness, as explained in the passage that this flows from the side of Chesed. So too David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 36:8), "How precious is Your kindness, O God; the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings. They shall be sated from the abundance of Your house, and You shall give them drink from the river of Your delights." And they explained in the Tikkunim (88a) the secret of "the river of Your delights"; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:86: And in Vayikra Rabbah, parashat "An ox or a sheep or a goat" (27:1), our sages, of blessed memory, said on this verse — Rabbi Elazar bar Menachem said: it is not written "Your delight" [ednecha] but "Your delights" [adanecha, plural], teaching that every single righteous person has his own individual Eden.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:87: He said at the end of the passage, "let not the foot of pride come upon me" — for whoever has within him a trace of the entry of pride, in the manner of a foot that comes and goes, let him not come there — in the manner of (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:88: Although the pleasantness that the righteous merit comes from the side of Chesed, nevertheless the aspect of judgment accompanies it, so that the utmost precision is exercised as to whether one is fit for that rank or not, as stated in the passage, "if it merits," etc., "and if it does not merit," etc.; and this is what is meant by (Psalms 36:11), "Draw out Your kindness to those who know You" — precisely.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:89: So too he said (Psalms 31:20), "How great is Your goodness, which You have hidden away for those who fear You, which You have worked for those who take refuge in You" — they explained in the Zohar, parashat Bereishit (7a), that "which You have worked for those who take refuge in You" is said of Gan Eden, where the righteous stand clothed in a garment resembling this world; see there. And the phrase "how great is Your goodness" is the secret of the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, created on the first day, which Moses made use of, and which He has hidden away for the righteous for the future to come, as the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:90: When a person wishes to discern the goodness of the World to Come through the affairs of this world, he should consider what was said at Elijah's wedding-canopy: three things are a semblance of the World to Come — Sabbath, sun, and marital union. — end of quotation. The explanation is that on the Sabbath the light revealed to us is a semblance of the World to Come, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Bereishit Rabbah 11:2): the light of a person's face on the Sabbath is not comparable to that of the weekdays. And likewise what they said in Tractate Shabbat (119a) about that gentile who asked why our Sabbath stew smells so good — they said to him, we have a spice, and its name is Sabbath, and whoever does not keep the Sabbath, his stew does not have this smell. And on the day of Sabbath, through the additional soul that comes, one will sense in his soul a wondrous delight, and if he is wise, through it the secrets of Torah will be revealed to him, as I have seen with my own eyes in my master, may his rest be in Eden, and other sages like him. Further, on the matter of the Sabbath as a semblance of the World to Come, we elaborated in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 2; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:91: Likewise the sun is a semblance of the hidden light — for just as a person cannot gaze upon it when it is at its full strength, so a person cannot withstand the secret of the hidden light in this world; and in the future to come it will be revealed to the souls in the lower Gan Eden — "the sun of righteousness with healing in its wings" — as the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, parashat Vayakhel 211a), a passage we quoted in the Gate of Fear, chapter 13. And likewise, regarding the future, it is said of the sun (Isaiah 30:26), "and the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:92: Marital union — that physical pleasure is one-sixtieth of the pleasure of the World to Come; and in Tractate Berachot (57b) they said that this union [in the analogy] refers only to the joining of the openings [i.e., a mere touching, not the pleasure itself].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:93: A further semblance for discerning the pleasure of the World to Come is the matter of pleasant fragrance, as the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained regarding the fragrance we smell at the conclusion of the Sabbath — he said (Zohar, parashat Vayakhel 208b): come and see, fragrance is the sustenance of the soul, because it enters the soul and not the body — "and he smelled the smell of his garments"; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:94: Let us return to the exposition of the verse we were engaged in, regarding "He will do for one who waits for Him." The Rashbi, of blessed memory, explained (Zohar, parashat Chayei Sarah 130b): come and see, happy are the righteous, for whom so much good is hidden away for that world, and there is no place more inward than that reserved for those who know the secret of their Master and know how to cling to Him every day. Of these it is written (Isaiah 64:3), "No eye has seen, O God, besides You, what He will do for one who waits for Him." What is meant by "waits for Him"? As it is said (Job 32:4), "he waited for [chikkah] Job with words." And these are they who press themselves into matters of wisdom, and search and wait for it, to know the clarity of the matter and to know their Master — these are they of whom their Master is praised every day; these are they who enter among the holy supernal ones, and these enter all the gates above and none can prevent their hands — happy is their portion in this world and in the World to Come. — end of quotation. And when you examine this whole rank carefully, they are those who debate in divine wisdom to know the secret of the matter in its proper form, as explained at the beginning of the passage, and as it also says afterward, "to know the clarity of the matter and to know their Master."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:95: Therefore a person must improve his deeds and always be fearful lest sin cause him to become unfit for that supernal rank, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot, first chapter, 4a), that David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 27:13), "Had I not believed to see the goodness of the Lord," etc. Our sages, of blessed memory, said: it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosi: why are there dots over the word "lulei" [had I not]? David said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the universe, I am confident in You that You will pay a good reward to the righteous in the future to come; but I do not know whether I have a portion among them or not. — end of quotation. And it says further there that he feared lest sin cause it. And if David the king, peace be upon him, was afraid and was not confident in his deeds, what shall one say who is full of countless sins, and on what shall he rely, if not that he return in complete repentance until his day of death, and even so — perhaps.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:96: One who is confident that he will merit the goodness of the World to Come without effort in deeds is a fool and a simpleton — for one who did not labor on the eve of the Sabbath, what will he eat on the Sabbath? For this is impossible; according to how much a person labors, so he eats — and the goodness of the World to Come is attained only through great diligence and industry. Concerning this Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 13:4), "the sluggard's soul desires and has nothing, but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat" — meaning, one who desires to delight in the World to Come in that pleasure, but does not perform deeds fit to attain that light, his soul is sluggish, in the manner of their saying, if he did not labor what shall he eat; "but the soul of the diligent," who are diligent in engaging with Torah and commandments, "shall be made fat" in the World to Come from supernal delight, for according to what he has done, he shall eat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:97: Although one labors, he should not rely upon his deeds, but rather upon the supernal kindness with which the Holy One, blessed be He, will reward him, as brought in Chovot HaLevavot, in the Gate of Trust (ch. 4), in these words: one of the pious used to say, a person cannot attain the reward of the World to Come through his deeds if a precise accounting is made of what he owes God for His favors upon him; rather, it is through the kindness of God upon him. Therefore, do not rely upon your deeds. And David said regarding this (Psalms 62:13), "and Yours, O Lord, is kindness, for You repay each man according to his deed." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:98: He further wrote there, on the manner of trust in the World to Come, in these words: the correct manner of trust in God is that one should occupy himself with the causes that bring him to the ranks fit for the pious — namely, to conduct himself with the qualities of the ascetics who despise this world, to remove his love and preference from his heart and exchange it for love of Him, blessed be He, to submit himself to Him and delight in Him, to be astonished at the world and its inhabitants, to conduct himself in the manner of the prophets and the pious, and his heart should be confident in God that He will be kind to him just as He was kind to them, [granting him a share] in the World to Come. But whoever relies upon God to grant him this without effort in deeds is a fool and simpleton, and he resembles those of whom it is said, they act as Zimri and seek reward like Pinchas. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:99: Among the signs of people of this great rank is that the servants of the Creator acknowledge the service of the Creator, and that endurance in time of trial and distress becomes light in their eyes compared to the fulfillment of the Creator's commandments, blessed be He — as you know from "God tested Abraham," and the matter of Chananiah, Mishael, and Azariah in the fiery furnace, and Daniel in the lion's den, and the ten martyrs of the kingdom, and one who chose death in service of the Creator over life in his rebellion, and poverty over wealth, and illness over health, and distress over peace — and submitted himself to the judgment of the Creator and desired His decree — such a person is worthy of the Creator's kindness upon him in the pleasantness of the World to Come, of which the verse says (Proverbs 8:21), "to cause those who love me to inherit substance, and I will fill their treasuries." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:100: Similarly, to the strictness my master, may his rest be in Eden, applied to the acquisition of the goodness of the World to Come, they applied strictness in the Zohar (parashat Bereishit 4a) regarding [spiritual] qualities, in the story of Rabbi Chiya, when he saw Rabbi Shimon: in these words: meanwhile, he saw several great and supernal wings, and Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Elazar his son ascended upon them, and ascended to the academy of the firmament, and all these wings awaited them. He saw that they were being renewed, restored in their splendor and light, greater than the light of the splendor of the sun. Rabbi Shimon opened and said: let Rabbi Chiya enter and see how the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to renew the faces of the righteous for the time to come. Happy is he who enters here without shame, and happy is he who stands in that world like a firm pillar in all things. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:101: And further there: the voice returned as before and said: supernal, hidden, concealed ones, open-eyed, who roam throughout the whole world — look and see the ones below, sleeping, shut up in their holes; awaken! Which of you turns darkness into light and tastes the bitter as sweet, before you come here? Which of you awaits every day the light that shines at the time the King commands the hind, and the King becomes more honored than all the kings of the world? Whoever does not anticipate this every day in that world has no portion here. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:102: As for what it says, "happy is he who enters here without shame" — this shame may occur in one of two ways: first, that he should not feel shame entering the King's palace on account of his evil deeds — for this is the shame that grips people, as it says, "let us lie down in our shame, and let our disgrace cover us, for we have sinned against the Lord our God" (Jeremiah 3:25) — will he not be ashamed and humiliated when the ledgers of his evil deeds are shown before all the pious and righteous in Gan Eden, as we quoted stories of judgments in Gan Eden in the Gate of Fear, chapter 13; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:103: The second: shame will also befall him if he did not engage in Torah as is fitting; and so the Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, parashat Pekudei, Second Hall, 247b), in these words: this holy Chayah stands, and when the soul ascends and reaches it, it then asks it about the secret of its Master's wisdom, and according to that wisdom that it pursued and clung to, so is its reward given. And if it was able to cling and did not cling, it pushes it outside, and it does not enter, and it stands beneath that hall in shame; and when those Seraphim beneath it flap their wings, they all strike with their wings and burn it — and it is burned and not burned, and stands and does not stand — and thus it is judged every day, shining and not shining. And even though it has good deeds, [it suffers] because it has no reward in that world like those who labor in wisdom to gaze upon the honor of their Master; and there is no measure to the reward of those who know wisdom regarding the honor of their Master. Happy is their portion in this world and in the World to Come, as it is written (Proverbs 3:13), "Happy is the man who finds wisdom, and the man who attains understanding." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:104: As for what it says, "happy is he who stands in that world like a firm pillar in all things" — the intent is that he was strong in divine service like a strong pillar that does not waver, so that if he began performing a certain service, such as rising early for synagogue or rising at midnight, he would not abandon that service under any circumstances in the world, and he would bind an oath upon himself to fulfill that commandment, as David the king, peace be upon him, said in the psalm (Psalms 15:1), "Lord, who shall sojourn in Your tent, who shall dwell in Your holy mountain" — and he said that one of the qualities is "he swears to his own hurt and does not change," and Radak and the other commentators explained that the meaning of "swears to his own hurt" is to hurt his own body through fasting and mourning practices, abstaining from pleasures, and likewise diminishing his purse for charity and commandments and the like, and not changing what he has vowed even though it hurts his body — in the manner David said (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to keep Your righteous judgments."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:105: In this manner too is (Avot 3:13), "vows are a fence for abstinence" — in general, to be firm. And likewise in the Tikkunim (21a), regarding "whoever fixes a place for his prayer" — for as souls act, so the Shechinah dwells with them: a soul that is fixed in prayer or in Torah is a place for the Shechinah to dwell in it; but a soul that has no fixedness in prayer or Torah, but only happens upon it by chance, likewise the Shechinah dwells upon it by chance, and this is "when a bird's nest chances before you." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:106: Further, "firm" means that he should not be defeated by his evil inclination even in the slightest of matters — for if he is defeated in one thing, he will be defeated in another and will separate from his service. Rabbeinu Bachya, in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Abstinence, ch. 5), likened the matters of service and abstinence to crystal beads strung on a thread — for if you loosen one bead from it, they will all scatter and their stringing will be ruined; and he said, therefore, strive to be careful with all of them, and then you will have help for the rest of them, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:2), that one commandment draws another commandment. And the sage said, regarding the succession of good things one after another (Proverbs 8:34), "Happy is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my gates" — he said first "listens," then "to watch," and then "to guard" [the sequence in the verse]. — end of quotation. This is what the Rashbi, peace be upon him, said concisely, "like a firm pillar in all things" — meaning, in all the commandments and matters of service that a person can fulfill; he must be strong in all of them so as not to be defeated.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:107: He further said, "open-eyed ones, who roam throughout the whole world" — my master, may his rest be in Eden, explained that these are the seven eyes of the Lord that roam throughout the whole earth in the world, to watch over the deeds of human beings, as we elaborated at length in the Gate of Fear. "Look and see" — that they watch below, and here the matter pauses.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:108: He further said, "those below, sleeping" — meaning the lower human beings who are asleep in the sleep of blindness — awaken to the service of the Creator! "Which of you turns darkness to light" — meaning, to turn judgment into mercy, which is when a person overcomes his evil inclination — for the evil inclination stems from the left and the good inclination from the right, and when the evil inclination is subdued beneath the good inclination, the left is incorporated within the right, and darkness turns to light and bitter to sweet. And there is one who explained that it means to turn the attribute of night, which is darkness, into light, through engaging in Torah, which is called light — and this too is correct.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:109: "Which of you awaits every day the light that shines," etc. — my master, may his rest be in Eden, explained that this is a warning to those who rise from midnight onward to engage in Torah, that they should not return to sleep, but rather must remain awake and wait for the light that shines, etc., namely at "the darkness of morning," as explained in parashat Beshalach (46a).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:110: Thus it has been explained how many things a person must do to merit that supernal pleasantness, and their essence is rising at midnight to study Torah until daybreak, as it says, "whoever does not anticipate this every day has no portion here." This quality is stated at the end of the passage because rising at midnight is not compatible with having evil deeds — for the qualities require mutual correspondence with one another; therefore repentance and [good] deeds must come first, so that he overcomes his inclination and the other matters, along with the quality of rising early to study Torah. Thus far have come the general reflections that a person is obligated to examine in order to love his Creator.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:111: When you examine all the aspects mentioned, you will find that all of them stem from the side of Chesed — whether in the creation of the world, as it says (Psalms 89:3), "I said, the world shall be built with kindness"; whether in the creation of man through a holy soul; whether in the aspect of sustenance, from the side of Chesed, as it says (ibid. 136:25), "He gives bread to all flesh, for His kindness is forever"; whether in the matter of death, of which it is said "very good" for the reason we explained; whether in his reward in the World to Come, "and Yours, O Lord, is kindness" (ibid. 62:13), and likewise (ibid. 57:11), "for Your kindness is great above the heavens," as explained above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:112: All the other particulars, too, are all from the side of Chesed — such as the matter of the four who must give thanks, which our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 54b), in these words: Rav Yehudah said: four must give thanks — those who go down to the sea, those who travel through deserts, one who was ill and recovered, and one who was imprisoned; and of all of them it is written, "let them thank the Lord for His kindness." And the place where Chesed is revealed more than in all of them is in the one who was ill and recovered, for he reaches the gates of death — as Elihu explained regarding the sick (Job 33:20), "and his life loathes bread, and his soul, food of desire"; "his flesh is consumed away from sight," etc.; "and his soul draws near to the pit," etc.; "if there is for him an angel, an intercessor, one among a thousand, to declare for man his uprightness, then He is gracious to him and says, deliver him from going down to the pit." And our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Shabbat 32a) that even if nine hundred and ninety-nine argue for his guilt and only one argues in his favor, he is saved; see there. This surely indicates the complete kindness [of the Holy One, blessed be He] toward His creatures.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:113: When a person examines all the particular kindnesses that the Holy One, blessed be He, has done for him, from the day he came out into the air of the world until he stood at the stature of a man, they cannot be counted for their abundance — such that he is obligated to the Creator in service out of complete love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:114: A further aspect of Chesed is that He, blessed be He, receives a person in repentance after he has sinned, as it is said, "His right hand is stretched out to receive the penitent" — meaning that Chesed extends even to the kelipah, to raise the soul up from there. This matter is revealed in the Torah (Leviticus 14:3), "and the priest shall go out to outside the camp to cleanse the leper"; and even in Gehinnom (Psalms 139:10), "even there Your hand shall lead me, and Your right hand shall hold me" — meaning, "Your hand shall lead me" is the hand of judgment, leading me there in Gehinnom for the cleansing of the soul, "and Your right hand shall hold me," that it may ascend from there — and this is "His right hand is stretched out." I heard the root of this teaching from my master, may his rest be in Eden.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 6:115: Rabbeinu Bachya elaborated at length, in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Self-Reckoning, ch. 3), on many other particulars of God's kindnesses to man — whether in his creation from nothing into being, whether in the perfection of his limbs, all of them whole, whether in the completion of his intellect and the like — all of which is supernal kindness, even though he is obligated by strict judgment on account of his sins. And even one who is missing one of his limbs should accept his afflictions with love, as will be further explained, that one is obligated to accept afflictions with love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Love 7:1: This chapter shall be an explanation of the Holy One, blessed be He's, love for Israel. It says in Tanna Devei Eliyahu (Rabbah, ch. 25), in these words: "I am the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:2) — blessed is the Omnipresent, who chose Israel out of all the nations, out of all who come into the world, and out of all the works of His hands, and acquired them as a complete acquisition, as sons and as servants, and called them by His own name. Many times He speaks with them, and when He speaks with them He speaks with them in love — that He loved them with the joy that He rejoiced in them. Therefore a person is obligated to say: when will my deeds reach the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who acquired this world and the World to Come and the days of the Messiah only through good deeds and the study of Torah? Therefore a person is obligated to say, the world was created for my sake. By what does a person acquire [merit before] his Father in Heaven? Through deeds and the study of Torah. And the Holy One, blessed be He, grants him as an acquisition this world, the days of the Messiah, and the World to Come. A person acquires [merit before] his Father in Heaven through love, through brotherhood, through friendship, through truth, through peace, through much sitting [in study], through minimizing business dealings, through the give-and-take of Torah, through attending upon the sages, through the give-and-take of the Talmud, through humility of bearing, through modesty, through [answering] "no" as "no," and "yes" as "yes."
